description: Turning satellite data into smarter harvests! Backend and AI/ML engineer (Node.js, AWS, Python). Want to win? Join me if you're a frontend developer, designer or data wizard.
summary:
A farmer picks what to plant next season, and that one choice shapes the soil and the water for years afterwards. Most tools score one crop, in one year, at one place. The benefit of rotating crops never shows up that way. It only exists across a sequence.

FieldShift runs the soil itself forward through 41 years of real NASA weather, carrying water, nitrogen, carbon and crop residue from one season into the next, for every rotation a field can actually support. Pick any point on Earth and get ranked options and a printable one-page plan in about forty seconds.

The part we are proudest of is what we caught in our own work. USDA crop maps showed that none of our five US test fields were growing what we had assumed, and four were not farmland at all. One sat inside Wichita. We moved every site onto verified cropland and re-ran the whole project. All twelve validation checks are published in the app, including the two we fail.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Pick a field on a map. FieldShift fetches 41 years of daily NASA POWER weather for that exact point, looks up the soil, enumerates every crop rotation physically possible there, and simulates each one day by day through all 41 years. About a million simulated days per field. It then shows the rotations that are not beaten on any measure, and makes the trade-off between them explicit.

The field is not a blank slate each season. Soil water, nitrogen, carbon, surface residue and pathogen history carry forward from one crop into the next, so a legume appears as a nitrogen credit to the crop that follows and a thirsty crop appears as a cost to whatever comes after it.

Seven published models are chained together: FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration, the FAO-56 dual crop coefficient water balance, SCS curve number runoff, RothC-26.3 soil carbon, a nitrogen balance coupled to RothC's own carbon flows, RUSLE erosion, and a sequence simulator that carries state across the whole rotation. Flooded rice runs on a separate ponded balance, because under standing water the dual coefficient machinery describes nothing real.

Candidates are enumerated exhaustively, reduced by cyclic equivalence, then filtered on pathogen return intervals and calendar feasibility. Every rejection is counted and explained.

Simulating one site takes about a minute. Re-ranking it against a farmer's stated priorities takes 10 milliseconds. So the physics is precomputed and the preference is live, and the answer moves the instant a priority changes.

WHAT BENEFITS IT HAS

It compares a farmer's actual options on their actual field, rather than offering generic advice. At Finney County, Kansas, 176 rotation cycles were examined, 79 were feasible, and two beat current practice on every objective: production 1.38 to 2.02 tonnes of dry matter per hectare per year, soil carbon gain 0.101 to 0.283, bare ground 61.6 percent of the year down to 21.5, wind erosion exposure 653 down to 382.

It reports the bad years rather than the average year, because nobody farms an average year.

It says when there is no improvement. At two of our six sites nothing beats current practice, and the tool says so instead of inventing a recommendation.

Every recommendation carries an evidence card naming the datasets, the equations, what validation showed and what is unknown. Confidence is set by the weakest source, never the average.

The final output is a printable one-page plan: a month-by-month calendar, the handful of numbers that change, and the risks counted from 41 years of weather. Plain HTML with print CSS and no JavaScript, so it prints identically anywhere.

INTENDED IMPACT

The target is a farmer facing a resource they are drawing down faster than it refills. In Sangrur district, Punjab, we measured the water table falling 1.167 metres per year across 20 government observation wells with records up to 27 years. Every one was falling. Seven rotations beat the current rice and wheat system on every objective; the cheapest in water replaces one rice year in three with a rainfed legume, cutting irrigation from 1,961 to 1,489 millimetres per year, a 24 percent saving, while producing slightly more food. That field is 2.5 hectares, so this is aimed at smallholders rather than agribusiness.

Because the engine runs on globally available inputs, it works anywhere on Earth, not only where a soil survey exists.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Python 3.11, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy and pandas on the back end. The interface is a single HTML file with Leaflet and no build step. NASADEM elevation tiles are read directly as raw big-endian 16-bit integers, so there is no heavy geospatial stack and the whole project runs on a laptop.

Data: NASA POWER, NASADEM, MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI via NASA AppEEARS, USDA SSURGO, ISRIC SoilGrids, USDA NASS QuickStats, USDA Cropland Data Layer via the Microsoft Planetary Computer, gridMET, and CGWB groundwater records via India-WRIS.

Parameter tables cover 33 crops, 19 soilborne pathogens and 12 USDA soil texture classes, validated on load so bad agronomy raises an error rather than passing silently. 827 automated tests run on every change.

An AI coding assistant wrote the large majority of the code, tests under human direction. No AI model makes or influences a recommendation at runtime. There is no language model in the decision path, because an agronomist cannot audit a sentence a language model generated.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

The central insight is that a rotation benefit does not exist crop by crop. It only exists across a sequence. The obvious way to build this is a scoring table, points per crop for water and nitrogen and erosion, summed. We deliberately did not. A scoring table cannot represent sequence, so it cannot see the thing rotation actually is, and it can never produce a downside. Scoring happens only at the last step, on simulated outputs.

Splitting the expensive half from the cheap half, so physics is precomputed and preference is live, is what makes exploring trade-offs feel immediate.

Honesty is computed rather than asserted. One NASA POWER cell covers 270,400 hectares against a 2.5 hectare Punjab field, a ratio of 108,160 to 1, printed on the card. Confidence takes the minimum across sources. A region with no yield record cannot claim validation: it is refused in the constructor and there is a test for it.

Most unusually, we validated our own fieldwork. Using USDA's Cropland Data Layer, independent of the satellite data we validate against, we asked whether each site was actually a field growing the rotation we modelled. None of the five US sites matched and four were not farmland at all; one sat in built-up Wichita. We moved every site onto verified cropland and re-ran the entire project.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Being wrong in a believable way was the main risk, so most of the effort went into trying to disprove ourselves. Twelve independent checks: five pass, five partial, two fail. All twelve are shown in the app with the command that reproduces each, including the failures.

Twenty-three errors have been found in our own model, every one of which produced confident, plausible, wrong output before it was caught.

We refused to tune. Our flooded-rice model, which the whole Punjab result rests on, was tested against Arkansas, where USDA publishes applied water. We asked 77 percent too much. Rebuilding the season model found three more bugs and it still fails at 53 percent over. Percolation, irrigation efficiency or the crop coefficients would each have reproduced the published figure with a plausible-looking number, and each would have destroyed the meaning of the agreement.

Limits are stated on the output, not in a footnote. No farmer has used this; zero field trials, and that is the largest limitation. No prices, because we will not invent market data. No methane from flooded paddy, so our carbon figure flatters rice. Erosion is water only, and wind is reported as an exposure index because quantifying it properly needs data no dataset carries.

Guardrails warn rather than refuse, using frequencies from the record such as killing frost during grain fill in 7 of 41 years, because a screen that refuses freely removes options a farmer may have good local reasons to want.

Every output ends the same way: FieldShift supports a decision; it does not make one.
